AI coding agents can waste time and tokens relearning the same lessons. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that builds on past sessions to cut costs while maintaining task success. It’s a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively.

events.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer

arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. During the time these agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code (I counted), we merged over 300 commits in the actual curl project. We actually improved curl during these a little more than three weeks. A little over 200 bugfixes actually. 200 bugfixes that none of those rust rewrites have. We also fixed a few vulnerabilities. In another month we have done another 200 and maybe fixed a few more vulnerabilities. Will these clones keep up?

— Daniel Stenberg, Actual curl rewrites in Rust

As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience.

Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

1. Use generative AI when you don't need generative AI

Every time there’s a new technology, I can hear the collective sigh of senior engineers everywhere: “Not everything is a nail.” Generative AI isn’t an exception — its seemingly limitless capabilities only exacerbate the tendency to use generative AI for everything.

A team pitched me the idea of using generative AI to optimize energy consumption. They fed a household’s list of energy-intensive activities and hourly electricity prices into an LLM, then asked it to create a schedule to minimize energy costs. events.excerpt: # Release v5.23.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling2 Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs, and it is intended for use in English and other languages and across multiple coding languages. Its language backbone has 48 mixture-of-experts decoder layers, each routing tokens to 8 of 384 experts, for 594B total and 17B active parameters. It keeps the Inkling decoder (learned relative attention, short causal convolutions, mixture-of-experts layers) and adds block attention residuals, gated attention with a learned sink, and dynamic key/value convolutions. Images are encoded by a Perception Encoder-based vision transformer and projected into the language model embeddings, one embedding per 40x40 pixel patch. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) * Add inkling2 (#50682) by @guarin in [#50682](https://github.com/huggingface/transforme

The PSF end-of-year fundraiser

With my Python Software Foundation board director hat on: we've launched our end-of-year fundraiser for the non-profit that supports Python development and the Python community.

If your company or your work benefits from Python, please consider donating this year!

The PSF looks after the IP behind Python, operates PyPI, sponsors core developer sprints, supports community events (including running PyCon US every year), and employs a small and excellent staff team to keep everything running.

We also operate the Developers in Residence program, which now includes three security developers (welcome, Brett Smith) focused on helping secure Python, PyPI, and the wider ecosystem.

Tags: python, psf

events.excerpt:
### Features

* **api:** add beta support for the billing_policy request parameter
* **api:** add contract_spend_limit_reached error code to messages
* **api:** add error codes for linked billing refusals
* **api:** add the user_profile_billing_not_authorized error code
* **api:** add webhook events for external key failure and recovery


### Bug Fixes

* **client:** stop reporting failed aiohttp connections as timeouts
* **types:** keep deprecated model aliases and the types nested under them working


### Chores

* **api:** rename error data models, deprecating the old names
* **docs:** clarify which AWS KMS keys a workspace can use on Claude Platform on AWS
* **docs:** clarify which credential work get, update and list accept
* **docs:** clarify which uploads a plugin pin holds back
* **docs:** note that a plugin scan's reason also covers errored scans

  `content_scan.reason` on an errored scan now says why there is no verdict. It is not a security finding, so code that treats any `reason` as a concern should also check `status`.

* **internal:** don't report moved classes as breaking changes


### Documentation

* name each SDK's own types in rename deprecations
